summary: A Healthline article comparing cold and hot showers, noting that each has health pros and cons. Cold showers may calm itchy skin, wake you up, increase circulation, ease post-workout soreness, possibly aid weight loss, and improve skin and hair, with few cons, though they may not suit people who are already cold or sick. Hot showers can relieve respiratory symptoms, help with blemishes and muscle relaxation, but can dry skin, worsen eczema, cause itching and raise blood pressure. The article recommends a lukewarm shower with moisturizer, or a contrast shower alternating one minute of cold and hot water for three to five cycles.
one_line: Healthline article weighing the pros and cons of cold versus hot showers and recommending a lukewarm or contrast shower approach.
key_facts: The article was medically reviewed by Alana Biggers, M.D., MPH and written by Sara Lindberg, updated on March 21, 2023.
Cold showers may help calm itchy skin, according to Adam Friedman, MD.
A cold shower's shock increases oxygen intake, heart rate and alertness.
Cold water constricts circulation on the body's surface, causing blood in deeper tissues to circulate faster to maintain ideal body temperature.
Some fat cells, such as brown fat, generate heat by burning fat when the body is exposed to cold, and are mostly situated around the neck and shoulder area according to Gerrit Keferstein, MD.
Dr. Jacqueline Schaffer, MD says cold water tightens and constricts blood flow, which gives skin a healthier glow.
Unlike hot water, cold water doesn't dry out the sebum layer, a naturally lubricated barrier that protects skin and hair.
Cold showers may not be a good idea if you're already cold or if you're sick, since the cold temperature might be too hard on your immune system.
Standing in a hot shower with steam has long been used as a natural remedy to reduce cold and cough symptoms.
Hot showers activate the parasympathetic nervous system, which makes us tired, according to Keferstein.
Hot water damages keratin cells in the epidermis, creating dry skin and preventing cells from locking in moisture, says Schaffer.
Higher temperatures can worsen conditions like eczema.
Friedman says heat can cause mast cells (which contain histamine) to release their contents in the skin and cause itching.
Friedman says the ideal approach is a lukewarm shower followed by applying moisturizer to damp skin after bathing.
A contrast shower, developed by Dr. Sebastian Kneipp, alternates one minute of cold water and one minute of hot water for three to five cycles.
